quiz_cv:1.q: The lines from X end on small openings in the wall of this capillary. In which organ does the lecture place this type of capillary?
quiz_cv:1.r: Rows of small pores (fenestrae) in an otherwise complete wall mark a fenestrated capillary, which the slide lists for intestines, endocrine glands and kidneys (p. 1089, p. 1090). Muscle and brain have continuous capillaries; spleen and bone marrow have sinusoids.
quiz_cv:1.alt: Colour drawing of a capillary cut open with two red cells inside; two lines run from a label X to the wall.

quiz_cv:10.q: Two profiles of the same type of small vessel are shown in connective tissue. In the lecture's order of flow, into which vessel does blood pass next?
quiz_cv:10.r: A small lumen ringed by a few layers of smooth muscle (1 to 5 in the table, p. 1100), with endothelial nuclei bulging into the lumen, is an arteriole (p. 1106). The order of flow is arteriole, capillary, postcapillary venule, collecting venule, muscular venule (p. 1111).
quiz_cv:10.alt: H&E micrograph of two small thick-walled vessel profiles surrounded by pink connective tissue.

quiz_cv:11.q: A narrow blood vessel has a lumen of about 150 micrometers, 2 layers of smooth muscle in its tunica media and no elastic lamina. How is it classified?
quiz_cv:11.r: The table gives the muscular venule a lumen of about 100 to 200 micrometers, 1 to 2 layers of smooth muscle and no elastic lamina (p. 1100, p. 1129). An arteriole has a lumen under 100 micrometers and a collecting venule has no smooth muscle.

quiz_cv:12.q: In this blood-filled vessel, the yellow arrow marks the outermost tunic, which is thicker than the tunic beneath it. According to the lecture, what does the arrowed tunic contain?
quiz_cv:12.r: This is a medium vein: thin media, thicker adventitia (p. 1112). The tunica adventitia is connective tissue plus blood vessels plus nerves, and it is thinner in arteries and thicker in veins (p. 1098).
quiz_cv:12.alt: H&E cross-section of a vessel packed with red cells; a yellow arrow points at the pale outer layer of its wall.

quiz_cv:13.q: This section shows part of a vessel wall with the lumen at the left. The yellow arrow marks one of many bundles cut in cross-section. Which vessel and layer contain such bundles?
quiz_cv:13.r: Large veins such as the vena cava have a thin tunica media, while the thick tunica adventitia contains longitudinal bundles of smooth muscle and vasa vasorum (p. 1113; table p. 1100).
quiz_cv:13.alt: H&E micrograph of a thick vessel wall made of many rounded pink bundles separated by red strands; a yellow arrow points at one bundle.

quiz_cv:14.q: The yellow arrow marks a thin flap projecting into the lumen of this vessel. According to the lecture, what does this flap do?
o: Shunts blood from arteriole to venule
Closes the capillary bed at its entry
Filters lymph before it enters blood
Keeps blood flowing toward the heart
quiz_cv:14.r: The flap is a valve of a vein: unidirectional blood flow in veins is facilitated by valves (p. 1114). The table lists valves with the thin tunica intima of small to medium veins (p. 1100), and the handout places them in the extremities (p. 1139). The picture is an unseen image from an outside atlas.
quiz_cv:14.alt: Low-power stained section of a large folded vessel; a yellow arrow points at a thin strand lying in the lumen.

quiz_cv:17.q: The yellow arrow marks the mesothelium on the surface of this layer of the heart wall, which here holds abundant fat. To which layer of a blood vessel is this heart layer homologous?
quiz_cv:17.r: Mesothelium over adipose tissue is the epicardium (p. 1119), and the epicardium is homologous to the tunica adventitia (p. 1117, p. 1139). Endocardium matches the intima and myocardium the media.
quiz_cv:17.alt: Micrograph of a heart wall layer with a thin dark surface line, a wide zone of empty-looking round cells and dense muscle at the bottom; a yellow arrow points at the surface line.

quiz_cv:18.q: The yellow arrow marks the surface layer in this section of the heart wall, and large pale cells lie just beneath it. According to the handout, what does the arrowed layer consist of?
o: Cardiac muscle on a fibrous skeleton
quiz_cv:18.r: Purkinje fibers lie just under the endocardium (p. 1119), so the arrowed layer is the endocardium: an endothelium and an underlying thin layer of connective tissue, continuous with the tunica intima of vessels (p. 1141).
quiz_cv:18.alt: Micrograph of a heart wall with a dark fibrous surface band, groups of large pale cells under it and dense purple muscle below; a yellow arrow points at the surface band.

quiz_cv:19.q: The yellow arrow marks large pale cells lying between the chamber lining and the dark red muscle below. According to the lecture, what are these cells specialized for?
o: Storage of fat in the epicardium
quiz_cv:19.r: These are Purkinje fibers, the answer to the faculty practice question on this same image (p. 1131). They are specialized cardiac muscle cells that conduct impulses 5 times faster than the surrounding cells (p. 1120).
quiz_cv:19.alt: Stained section of heart wall with a blue surface layer, a zone of large pale pink cells and dark red muscle at the bottom; a yellow arrow points into the pale cells.

quiz_cv:2.q: This electron micrograph shows part of a capillary wall in the pancreas. The lines from X end at two sites where the endothelium thins to an opening. What spans each opening?
quiz_cv:2.r: The slide labels these sites 'fenestrae + diaphragm' (p. 1090), and the handout says the pores of fenestrated capillaries are spanned by a thin diaphragm, as in the intestine (p. 1136). Only the renal glomerulus lacks the diaphragm.
quiz_cv:2.alt: Black and white electron micrograph of a thin capillary wall between a lumen and a pericapillary space; two lines run from a label X to the wall.

quiz_cv:20.q: Which description from the lecture's muscle comparison fits the cells in this longitudinal H&E section?
quiz_cv:20.r: This is the myocardium in longitudinal section (p. 1119): faint cross-striations, one central nucleus per cell and branching fibers. The comparison slide describes cardiac muscle as branched networks, single nucleus, striated with intercalated discs (p. 1101); smooth muscle is tapered and non-striated.
quiz_cv:20.alt: H&E micrograph of pink fibers running left to right with scattered oval nuclei and small gaps holding red cells.

quiz_cv:5.q: How do the capillaries of the renal glomerulus differ from the fenestrated capillaries of the intestine, according to the lecture?
quiz_cv:5.r: The slide marks kidneys with an asterisk: no diaphragm, thick basement membrane (p. 1089). The handout agrees: open pores without a diaphragm, surrounded by a thick continuous basal lamina, in the renal glomerulus (p. 1136).

quiz_cv:6.q: This drawing shows a capillary in cross-section. According to the lecture slide, what is the role of the cell marked X?
o: Converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II
Anchors the vessel to connective tissue
quiz_cv:6.r: X is a pericyte, wrapped around the outside of the endothelium; the slide says pericytes help maintain the viability of endothelial cells (p. 1088). The handout says their function is not clear and that they may differentiate into smooth muscle or phagocytic cells (p. 1136). Angiotensin conversion and nitric oxide belong to the endothelial cell (p. 1093).
quiz_cv:6.alt: Coloured drawing of a small vessel in cross-section with a central lumen; several unlabelled arrows point at the wall and one arrow is marked X.

quiz_cv:7.q: Route 2 in this diagram lets blood pass from an arteriole to a venule without entering a capillary bed. Where does the lecture locate this arrangement?
quiz_cv:7.r: Route 2 is an arteriovenous anastomosis, which the slide places in the dermis (p. 1107); the handout says dermis of the skin of the hands and feet (p. 1136). Route 3 is the kidney pattern and route 4 is the liver portal pattern.
quiz_cv:7.alt: Diagram of a red arteriole and blue veins joined by four numbered vessel routes, with most labels removed.

quiz_cv:8.q: This vessel wall was stained to show elastic fibers, which appear as dark wavy lines. According to the lecture's vessel table, how much smooth muscle does its tunica media contain?
quiz_cv:8.r: Elastic lamellae running through the whole media mark an elastic (conducting) artery such as the aorta (p. 1103). The table gives elastic arteries 40 to 60 layers of smooth muscle and 40 to 60 elastic laminae throughout the media (p. 1100, same table on p. 1140). The picture is an unseen image from an outside atlas.
quiz_cv:8.alt: Micrograph of a thick vessel wall, lumen at lower left, filled with many dark wavy parallel lines and a pale outer layer.

quiz_cv:9.q: The yellow arrow marks a dark wavy line just beneath the lining of this vessel. According to the lecture's vessel table, which elastic laminae does this type of vessel have?
o: May or may not have internal
quiz_cv:9.r: A round vessel with a prominent wavy internal elastic lamina and a thick muscular media is a muscular (distributing) artery (p. 1104). The table gives it internal and external elastic laminae (p. 1100); 'may or may not have internal' is the arteriole and 'internal, vague' is the small to medium vein.
quiz_cv:9.alt: Stained cross-section of a round vessel with a thick wall; a yellow arrow points at a dark wavy line around the lumen.

quiz_cv_b:1.q: On the lecture's overview slide, which pairing describes the lymphatic system as opposed to the cardiovascular system?
quiz_cv_b:1.r: The overview slide sets blood, heart pump, circulates (cardiovascular) against lymph, no pump, unidirectional (lymphatic) (p. 1084). The double pump is the heart (p. 1085).

quiz_cv_b:10.q: Capillaries usually connect the arterial side to the venous side. In route 4 of this diagram a capillary bed lies between two veins; where does the lecture place this pattern, and what is it called?
quiz_cv_b:10.r: Route 4 is venule, capillary, venule (liver), the portal system (p. 1107), one of the special exceptions to the arterial-to-venous rule (p. 1085). The kidney pattern is arteriole, capillary, arteriole (route 3) and the arteriovenous anastomosis is in the dermis (route 2).
quiz_cv_b:10.alt: Diagram of small vessels with four numbered routes between a red vessel on the left and blue vessels on the right

quiz_cv_b:11.q: The yellow arrow marks the tissue that makes up most of the heart wall. To which layer of a blood vessel is this heart layer homologous?
quiz_cv_b:11.r: The arrowed tissue is cardiac muscle, the answer to the faculty practice question on this image (p. 1133), so the layer is the myocardium. The myocardium is homologous to the tunica media; endocardium matches the intima and epicardium the adventitia (p. 1117).
quiz_cv_b:11.alt: Light micrograph of part of the heart wall with large pale cells above and a dense red tissue below, which is marked by a yellow arrow

quiz_cv_b:12.q: The heart is built on a supporting framework called the cardiac skeleton. According to the lecture, what is this framework made of?
quiz_cv_b:12.r: The heart is built on a cardiac skeleton of high density collagen, connective tissue (p. 1117). Specialized cardiac muscle describes Purkinje fibers (p. 1120), and mesothelium with adipose tissue belongs to the epicardium (p. 1119).

quiz_cv_b:13.q: After a fatty meal, the lymph leaving the small intestine turns milky white. Which lymphatic function listed in the lecture explains this finding?
quiz_cv_b:13.r: The three listed functions are return of the excess 10% of interstitial fluid to blood, transport of lipids absorbed from the intestines, and immunologic support (p. 1122). Lipid in the lymph is what makes it milky.

quiz_cv_b:14.q: The red outpouchings on the cerebral arteries in this diagram are berry aneurysms. What does the lecture list as the contents of the tunic whose defect underlies them?
quiz_cv_b:14.r: Berry aneurysms are related to defects in the tunica media of cerebral arteries (p. 1126). The tunica media is smooth muscle, elastic fibers and the external elastic lamina; the intima holds the endothelium and internal elastic lamina, and the adventitia holds connective tissue, vessels and nerves (p. 1097).
quiz_cv_b:14.alt: Diagram of the arteries at the base of the brain with red outpouchings at several branch points, each with a percentage

quiz_cv_b:15.q: The right panel shows the dilated, tortuous leg veins of a common condition, beside normal veins on the left. According to the lecture, which two changes cause it?
o: Weak artery wall, lost valve function
Thick vein wall, lost elastic lamina
Weak vein wall, lost valve function
quiz_cv_b:15.r: Varicose veins are abnormally dilated, tortuous veins with valve insufficiency; they develop from weakness of the vein wall and loss of valve function, in about 15 to 20% of people, in the lower legs (p. 1127).
quiz_cv_b:15.alt: Drawing of two legs with an inset of straight veins on the left and an inset of twisted, widened veins on the right

quiz_cv_b:2.q: The dots on the wall of this capillary are vesicles, not pores, and its endothelium has no gaps. Which sites does the lecture list for this type?
quiz_cv_b:2.r: An unbroken wall with pinocytic vesicles is a continuous capillary, listed under muscle, skin, lung and brain (p. 1089; skin, lungs and blood-brain barrier on p. 1090). Intestine, endocrine and kidney are fenestrated; liver, spleen and bone marrow are sinusoidal.
quiz_cv_b:2.alt: Cutaway drawing of a capillary containing two red blood cells, with small dots scattered over its wall

quiz_cv_b:3.q: The wall of this capillary has wide gaps, and the vessel is larger than other capillaries. In the liver, what kind of cell does the lecture place in its lumen?
quiz_cv_b:3.r: A large capillary with a discontinuous endothelium is a sinusoidal capillary (liver, spleen, bone marrow). Kupffer cells are specialized immune cells located inside the blood channels and are present in the lumen (p. 1090).
quiz_cv_b:3.alt: Cutaway drawing of a wide capillary containing red blood cells, with large holes in its wall

quiz_cv_b:4.q: A tracer protein crosses a capillary endothelial cell inside membrane-bound vesicles. Which term on the lecture's exchange slide names this route?
quiz_cv_b:4.r: The exchange slide lists diffusion, filtration and vesicular transport, and gives transcytosis as the other name for vesicular transport (p. 1091). Diapedesis is the exit of cells by way of adhesion molecules (p. 1093).

quiz_cv_b:5.q: The yellow arrow marks a cell in this electron micrograph of a capillary. According to the lecture, what does this cell do?
o: Filters lymph before it enters blood
quiz_cv_b:5.r: The cell lining the lumen is the endothelial cell. It produces vasoactive compounds: nitric oxide for vasodilation and endothelin for vasoconstriction (p. 1093). Maintaining endothelial viability is the pericyte's role (p. 1088).
quiz_cv_b:5.alt: Electron micrograph of a capillary in cross-section with a yellow arrow on a large cell beside the lumen

quiz_cv_b:6.q: Two neighboring vessels are shown with two stains, and X and Y mark their lumens in the left panel. Which vessel is the artery, and which lecture rule identifies it?
quiz_cv_b:6.r: The tunica media is thicker in arteries and thinner in veins, while the adventitia is thinner in arteries and thicker in veins (p. 1098). The slide labels the lower vessel with the thick, dark-staining media as the artery and the upper one as the vein (p. 1099).
quiz_cv_b:6.alt: Two side-by-side panels of the same tissue in two stains, each showing an upper and a lower vessel wall; the lumens are marked X and Y

quiz_cv_b:7.q: In the lecture's vessel table, most vessels have a thin tunica intima. Which two vessels are listed with a thick tunica intima?
quiz_cv_b:7.r: The table gives a thick tunica intima only to elastic arteries (aorta) and large veins (vena cava); arterioles, muscular arteries, venules and small to medium veins are all listed as thin (p. 1100).

quiz_cv_b:8.q: Vessel X receives blood directly from postcapillary venules in the lecture's order of flow. According to the lecture's vessel table, how much smooth muscle does its tunica media contain?
quiz_cv_b:8.r: The order of flow is arteriole, capillary, postcapillary venule, collecting venule, muscular venule (p. 1111), so X is a collecting venule. The table gives it no smooth muscle and no elastic lamina (p. 1100, p. 1129); 1 to 2 layers is the muscular venule.
quiz_cv_b:8.alt: Light micrograph of connective tissue with several small blood vessels cut across; one is marked X

quiz_cv_b:9.q: The cells in this panel are tapered at both ends and are not striated. Which location and control does the lecture's muscle comparison list for this type?
quiz_cv_b:9.r: Tapered, single nucleus, non-striated cells are smooth muscle: walls of hollow visceral organs, involuntary (p. 1101). Cardiac muscle is in the walls of the heart and involuntary; skeletal muscle is attached to bones and voluntary.
quiz_cv_b:9.alt: Two small panels, a drawing and a micrograph, of elongated muscle cells, with a drawing of a single cell beneath

brief:
Cardiovascular Histology High-Yield Tables (Exam 3)

Cardiovascular System (Banerjee) was 23/32 on your September quiz, with capillaries the weakest part at 5/10. Page numbers are pages of the combined PDF: slides pp. 1079–1134, handout pp. 1135–1141. Everything is from those pages unless labeled (outside the slides).

1. The circuit and the vessel classes (LO 1)

Blood runs heart, elastic artery, muscular artery, arteriole, capillary, venule, small to medium vein, large vein, heart (pp. 1095, 1135).

System Fluid Pump Flow Page
Cardiovascular Blood Heart, a double pump Circulates 1084–1085
Lymphatic Lymph No pump One direction only 1084
Vessel Definition on the slide Page
Artery Carries blood away from the heart 1085
Vein Returns blood to the heart 1085
Capillary Connects the arterial side to the venous side, with special exceptions 1085
Type of microcirculation Route Where Page
Usual Arteriole, capillary bed, venule Most tissues 1107
Arteriovenous anastomosis Arteriole straight to venule, bypassing capillaries Dermis of the skin (hands and feet) 1107, 1136
Arterial portal Arteriole, capillary, arteriole Kidney 1107
Venous portal Venule, capillary, venule Liver 1107

The handout names two portal systems: the hepatic portal system (gut capillaries to liver sinusoids) and the hypophyseal portal system (hypothalamus capillaries down the pituitary stalk to the adenohypophysis) (p. 1136).

2. Capillaries (LO 1–2)

Capillaries and post-capillary venules are the exchange vessels: gases, metabolic waste, nutrients and hormones (p. 1087).

Part of the wall Fact Page
Endothelium Single layer; nuclei bulge into the lumen 1088, 1136
Basal lamina Thin 1088
Pericyte Wraps the outside of the endothelium; helps maintain endothelial cell viability 1088
Diameter About 7–9 microns, just wide enough for one red cell 1088, 1136
Hallmark under the electron microscope Many pinocytotic pits and vesicles, about 80 nm 1136

The handout says the pericyte's function is not clear and that it may become smooth muscle or a phagocytic cell (p. 1136). If a question quotes the slide, answer "maintains endothelial viability".

Capillary type Wall Where How to recognize it Page
Continuous No pores; pinocytotic vesicles Muscle, skin, lung, brain (blood-brain barrier), connective tissue Unbroken thin wall 1089–1090, 1136
Fenestrated Pores, each spanned by a thin diaphragm Intestine, endocrine glands Wall thins to regularly spaced openings 1089–1090, 1136
Fenestrated, kidney Pores with NO diaphragm; thick basement membrane Renal glomerulus Open pores over a thick basal lamina 1089, 1136
Sinusoid (discontinuous) Gaps between endothelial cells; basal lamina missing or discontinuous; up to 30–40 microns wide, irregular lumen Liver, spleen, bone marrow Wide, irregular channel 1089–1090, 1136
Fenestrated sinusoid Large fenestrated capillary Adrenal gland, adenohypophysis Wide and fenestrated 1089, 1136

Kupffer cells sit inside the lumen of liver sinusoids (p. 1090).

Exchange mechanism What crosses Detail Page
Diffusion Gases and lipid-soluble substances Straight across the plasmalemma 1137
Filtration Water and small molecules Through "leaky tight junctions", driven by hydrostatic versus oncotic pressure 1137
Vesicular transport (transcytosis) Large molecules over 9 nm, such as plasma proteins The main mechanism for large molecules; pinocytotic pits and vesicles; not energy dependent 1091, 1137
Transendothelial channels Molecules under 9 nm Formed by fusion of vesicles; spanned by diaphragms 1137

The slide says transendothelial channels carry both small and large molecules (p. 1092); the handout limits them to under 9 nm (p. 1137). Answer by the handout unless the question quotes the slide.

Endothelial cell function Detail (p. 1093)
Adhesion molecules Allow diapedesis
Vasodilation Nitric oxide (NO)
Vasoconstriction Endothelin
Clotting Anti-thrombogenic factors
Metabolic conversion Angiotensin I to II, which gives vasoconstriction

3. The three tunics (LO 2)

Every larger vessel has the same three coats; arteries and veins differ in which coat is thick (pp. 1097–1098).

Tunic Contains Arteries Veins
Intima Endothelium, subendothelial connective tissue, internal elastic lamina (IEL)
Media Smooth muscle, elastic fibers, external elastic lamina (EEL) Thicker Thinner
Adventitia Connective tissue, blood vessels (vasa vasorum), nerves Thinner Thicker
Compared with its companion artery, a vein has (p. 1139)
Less muscle
More connective tissue
Less elastic tissue
A larger lumen
Valves, in the extremities

4. The vessel table (LO 2)

This is his table on p. 1100, and his practice question (pp. 1128–1129) is answered straight from the smooth muscle column: count the layers of smooth muscle nuclei in the media.

Vessel Lumen Intima Smooth muscle in media Adventitia Elastic lamina
Arteriole Under 100 microns Thin 1–5 layers Thin May or may not have internal
Muscular (distributing) artery About 300 microns Thin Up to 40 layers Thin Internal and external
Elastic artery (aorta) Large Thick 40–60 layers Thin 40–60 throughout the media
Collecting venule Under 50 microns Thin None Thin None
Muscular venule About 100–200 microns Thin 1–2 layers Thin None
Small to medium vein About 200 to over 1000 microns Thin, with valves Thin or absent Thick Internal, vague
Large vein (vena cava) Large Thick Thin, up to several layers Thick, with many longitudinal smooth muscle bundles Internal
How to recognize it in an image Clue Page
Elastic artery Media packed with wavy elastic sheets; with an elastic stain, many dark wavy lines 1103
Muscular artery Scalloped dark internal elastic lamina just under the lining; thick muscular media 1104–1105
Arteriole Small round vessel, wall 1–5 muscle cells thick, lumen about as wide as the wall 1106
Venule or vein Thin wall, large collapsed or blood-filled lumen, next to a thicker-walled artery 1109–1112
Large vein Thin media; adventitia holds longitudinal smooth muscle bundles cut in cross-section, and vasa vasorum 1113
Valve Thin flap of intima projecting into a vein lumen; keeps flow toward the heart 1114

Order of flow through the small vessels: arteriole, capillary, post-capillary venule, collecting venule, muscular venule (p. 1111).

5. The heart (LO 3)

The heart wall is three layers built on a cardiac skeleton of dense collagenous connective tissue, and each layer matches a vessel tunic (pp. 1117, 1139).

Heart layer Homologous to Made of How to recognize it Page
Endocardium Tunica intima Endothelium on a thin connective tissue layer; thicker subendocardial connective tissue beneath The lining of the chamber; Purkinje fibers lie just under it 1119, 1141
Myocardium Tunica media Cardiac muscle; thin in atria, much thicker in ventricles; attached to the fibrous skeleton The bulk of the wall 1141
Epicardium (visceral pericardium) Tunica adventitia Mesothelium on the surface; subepicardial loose connective tissue with fat, vessels and nerves Outer surface with adipose tissue 1119, 1141
Muscle Shape Nuclei Striated Where Control
Cardiac Branched networks Single Yes, with intercalated discs Walls of the heart Involuntary
Smooth Tapered at each end Single No Walls of hollow visceral organs Involuntary
Skeletal Long and cylindrical Many Yes Attached to bones Voluntary

That table is p. 1101.

Purkinje fiber fact Detail Page
What it is A specialized cardiac muscle cell 1120
Speed Conducts impulses 5 times faster than surrounding cells 1120
Look Large, pale cells under the endocardium 1119, 1131
Result Gap junctions let the wave of depolarization start contraction at the apex 1120

The pericardial cavity is a potential space between visceral and parietal pericardium holding up to 50 mL of fluid (p. 1141). Before fish, cephalochordates had no heart, only muscular vessels (p. 1116).

6. Lymphatics and clinical points

Lymphatic vessels return fluid and plasma protein from the interstitium to the blood (p. 1141).

Lymphatic function Page
Return the excess 10% of interstitial fluid to the blood 1122
Transport lipids absorbed from the intestine 1122
Immunologic support 1122
Lymph capillary feature Detail Page
Start End blindly 1141
Wall A single layer of endothelium only 1141
Basal lamina Discontinuous or missing 1141
Pericytes None 1141
Anchoring Filaments (elastic fibers) tie the endothelium to the surrounding connective tissue 1124, 1141
Larger lymph vessel versus vein Detail (p. 1141)
Valves Many
Wall Thinner than a vein
Contents No red cells, only lymphocytes

All lymph is filtered by at least one lymph node before it re-enters the blood, through the thoracic duct and the right lymphatic duct (pp. 1125, 1141).

Clinical point Detail Page
Berry aneurysm Defect in the tunica media of cerebral arteries 1126
Varicose veins Abnormally dilated, tortuous veins with valve insufficiency; from weakness of the vein wall and loss of valve function; 15–20% of people, in the lower legs 1127

7. Faculty questions on the slides, and your September misses

Slide What it asked Answer on the slide
1129 A narrow vessel with 10 layers of smooth muscle Distributing artery (muscular venule 1–2, arteriole 1–5, collecting venule none, elastic artery 40–60)
1131 Identify the tissue at the arrow in the heart wall Purkinje fibers
1133 The muscle that makes up most of the heart Cardiac muscle
Area The fact you missed in September Page
Capillaries Fenestrated capillaries are found in the intestine 1089
Capillaries A diaphragm spans each fenestra 1136
Capillaries Transendothelial channels form by fusion of vesicles 1137
Capillaries Plasma proteins over 9 nm cross by vesicular transport 1137
Capillaries Renal glomerulus: fenestrated, no diaphragm, thick basal lamina 1089, 1136
Arteries Arteriole: 1–5 layers of smooth muscle, lumen under 100 microns 1100
Heart Endocardium is the chamber lining, with Purkinje fibers beneath it 1119
Heart Cardiac muscle: branched, single nucleus, striated, intercalated discs 1101
Lymphatics Lymphatic capillaries have no pericytes 1141
